[None]

Our guest this week is Jenny Fielding, co -founder and general partner of Everywhere Ventures. Jenny's a pre -seed investor with a fascinating background. She's a founder, lawyer by training, has lived in 12 countries, visited more than 100, and ran Techstars New York for many years. She's also the author of Venture Everywhere, a book which comes out in March. We talked about Jenny's strategy, why venture doesn't scale, and how everywhere is navigating the seed and AI markets. Please enjoy. Jenny, thanks for coming on the show.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thanks so much for having me.

[SPEAKER_01]
So your site says you're a generalist and your name firm is Everywhere Ventures, which sounds very expansive, but you do have a sweet spot. And maybe just to get started, can you tell listeners about what your focus is?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. So, mean, we're called Everywhere Ventures because we believe innovation's everywhere and we want to be where the best founders are, wherever they are. And so, as you can imagine, our portfolio is quite diverse. But we also feel that geography is becoming a lot less important in many ways, or maybe very important, however you look at it. But oftentimes we'll meet a founder and one founder will be in Austin and one will be in Indonesia and one will be in the UK. And it's like, well, where is that company base? So it might be a US C Corp, but the company is everywhere, right? Or is in different places? And their customer base might be diverse as well. So we believe, you know, we're pretty excited to be part of this kind of opening where geographies are becoming, you know, less important and we can really focus on what matters, which is really founders and founders finding interesting markets to sell into. So we're generalists. I think that our, what's interesting is that our deal flow, we're not, you know, outbound, we're not thesis driven, but our deal flow comes from our community of founders and operators who've all invested into us. So we have 500 founders and operators that have become LPs in our

[None]
fund.

[SPEAKER_00]
They're our eyes and ears on the ground and they're located around the world. And so our deal flow is really amongst all those interesting companies that are coming from that network.

[SPEAKER_01]
That's awesome. There's a chicken or the egg to that, right? Which is the bigger the LPB space in the network, the more deal flow, the better the deal flow where, I guess, if you go back in time, like my kids ask me sometimes like chicken or the egg, literally like, which came first answer the question, Papa, like for you, which was first coming up with the firm, building the network? How did they go in tandem?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, well, as many people know, I spent almost eight years at Techstars. And so as I was building there, I was developing not just the companies that I was investing in, but all the mentor pools and kind of like the larger Techstars ecosystem was really chock full of founders, operators, former founders, you know, people that had been in and around startups. So when I decided to start the firm, I'd already had kind of hundreds of people that I'd interacted with, you know, quite frequently. Less, you know, valuation, every, you know, every point really matters, if that makes sense. So again, it's like, it doesn't really matter if it's, you know, a six or an eight, but it does matter if it's a six or a 25, just because we write one collaborative check. [None]

You know, we focus on verticals that, you know, we think have staying power for the next, you know, 10 years that are helping with kind of what we call the resilience economy. [None]
so many people

So I love visiting them because I think they, you know, even though they're so far away from the U.S., they have like this incredible worldview. And they're just ambitious as hell. [SPEAKER_00]

[SPEAKER_01]
Hi, Joe again. Thanks for watching the show. If you'd like more of this in the future, subscribe to our channel. If you'd like to learn more about Seaplane Ventures, just check out seaplaneventures.com. Cheers.

Hello, my name is Simon, I'm CEO and co -founder of Pimlock. So we're not an advertising company, we're never going to monetize your data. We want to give you the latest tools to enjoy and manage your image and video collections without you having to relinquish control. Everybody's image collections are full of very dense and very descriptive private data and most people, I assume most people in this room don't really know what's in their image collections. Most people don't have the time nor the inclination to go through every image and watch every video but as you've seen here in the last two days the machine can now do that very quickly and it's not a big step for these companies that you're providing your images into to start providing that data to insurers, potential employers as well as harassing you with more annoying advertising and actually whoops and if like me you enjoy a occasional drink that's probably something you're not necessarily going to want everybody to know. The other thing about personal image collections is actually a bit of a goldmine for someone that wants to hack in and get some of your private data. So one very quick search on my last ten years worth of images, which is about 30,000 images for receipt. I got about 700 responses, I found pictures of six different people's passports, medical records, share certificates, bank cards, my Wi -Fi password, lots of things my wife would never want anyone to see and I genuinely didn't know I had any of those things stored. You know with the usage of smartphones for documenting and the fact these things then disappear quickly into cloud storage systems actually there's a huge amount of data set in people's image collections but they just don't think about. So we've created a solution, it's Google Photos in a private box. It sits at the edge of your network in your living room, not somebody else's. You bring it home, you can connect it to your local Wi -Fi network via the smartphone app, the box is going to find all your images and videos, it's going to index them and then very quickly from the comfort of your home you can start to enjoy your past memories and your images and videos without having to give control of those away to anybody. The box ships with over 300,000 pre -trained classifiers so you can find the people, the objects, the activities, the locations and the scenes that you want to but alongside that basic functionality we've also built in some more advanced features for people with more specialist data sets, so keen hobbyists and people. So you can go and you can create new classifiers, you can improve them and we also have some new navigation tools for navigating much larger sections of images based on swiping and tapping on the content within them. tap an image of my wife's face and we'll give you all the images of my wife. And actually the edge -based processing and storage market is seeing a major resurgence at the moment. Analysts are predicting a 24 % growth over the next five years and we certainly think Pimlock's in a very good position to take a good slice of that. So we have projections to bring a range of products to market through direct sales but also some white label licensing of our platform. So the first thing we're going to do is we're going to launch our new box in August. We have two versions. We have a small memory version for people that already have adequate storage at home and a larger memory version for those that don't. You'll be pleased to know the platform already works, the electronics and the PCBs already done. We've had functional prototypes working for six months in a rail of trial areas. So all we need to do now is look for manufacturing partners for ramp up and pressing go on the tooling. We raised our seed round last October. We're currently starting to have conversations around looking for series A to take us through ramp up and initial batch production. And we've got a very special and fantastic team. So we've got two of the leading academics from Oxford University on the AI side. We have Julian who's set up and run actually three different computer vision companies in London over the last 30 years. We have James who built the original Hawkeye ball tracking system. That happens to be a bit of a genius. And then myself who's got a range of experience from Nokia and connected camera space recently. So thank you.

So I think, like, if you build those networks and those connections, like, no one with a nice, like, background, no one knows where you are anyway.

[None]
I

[SPEAKER_00]
love it. The blurred or fake background gives us geographic independence. You use the word, I think, burst. And we're going to end our hour with you with some rapid -fire questions. And before we do that, I'm going to ask Kemi to put in the chat for everyone both the link to your book one more time and also a link to our feedback form. We'd love to hear what you think of today and how we can improve. So quick rapid -fire. Are you ready?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yes.

[SPEAKER_00]
Drumroll, please. What was the biggest surprise about writing a book?

[SPEAKER_01]
How antiquated and wacky the publishing industry is.

[SPEAKER_00]
Totally. I agree. What is something about leading a organization that you've changed your mind about? How to change your heart?

[SPEAKER_01]
That you needed kind of one singular charismatic leader. And I really think you can have much more distributed leadership.

[SPEAKER_00]
Oh, I love that. And what is one commonly held belief that you hold a contrary opinion about aside from what you just said?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. used to. Well, I also used to feel that solo founders were at a huge disadvantage. And I, over the last 10 years, have slowly evolved my thinking there. And I do think that, you know, it's actually kind of cool to build a company by yourself. And there's really great ways to do that collaboratively with other people.

[SPEAKER_00]
Awesome. Jenny Fielding, thank you so much for this. Thank you for the book. I'm going to dig in. And I thank you so much for your time and look forward to seeing you on the streets of New York in that black leather jacket very soon.

[None]
And thanks, everyone,

[SPEAKER_00]
for calling in. This has been wonderful. Thank you, Josh and the VC platform. We'll see you all soon.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thank you. That was super fun.

[SPEAKER_00]
Ciao.

[None]
Ciao.
documents.title: Co-founder of Everywhere Ventures Jenny Fielding - Cultivating an Everywhere Mindset

documents.text:
[SPEAKER_00]
Hey friends, thanks for joining me, Jim Baroud, to hear a few insights from leaders who represent our innovation ecosystem. Today's chat is with Jenny Fielding, the co -founder and managing partner at Everywhere Ventures and the author of the new book, Venture Everywhere.

[SPEAKER_01]
I'm a venture capitalist, and what that means is I invest in startups at the earliest stage of their journey. So just as they're getting going, sometimes even idea stage, we bet on founders, on their ideas, and on their potential. And previously I was an entrepreneur, so I've walked in those shoes and kind of taken a lot of the learnings, especially the hard ones, and parlayed it into my own style of investing in companies.

[SPEAKER_00]
Awesome. I look forward to hearing that story. Again, you're one of the preeminent investors and one of the, unfortunately, still a handful of, you know, a small amount of female investors in this space, but you're one of the OGs, obviously. And so delighted to have you talk about that a bit, but let's talk about that. mean, how does one go from high school, college to become a, you know, an investor? So take us through that journey.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, well, like to say I'm both an accidental entrepreneur and an accidental investor, and that seems to be the through line of my life is kind of stumbling into things, but not really seeking them. So started much more traditional. So I grew up in New York City. I ended up in law school. I worked in finance, kind of like took a very different path. And then one day I had an idea, not for a startup, actually, like, because that kind of terminology at the time wasn't even in my head. Like, most of my friends were bankers and consultants, and I just, like, didn't come from that, you know, that kind of tech ecosystem that really just didn't exist in New York at the time. But I had a problem that I wanted to solve. And like most entrepreneurs that I call empath entrepreneurs, right, so they're solving for their self, I was just trying to, you know, figure this thing out for myself. Well, that kind of turned into getting co -founders, turned into starting a company in my living room and growing that company to more than 100 people, running it for a number of years and having an exit. So very accidental, again, didn't start out seeking to be an entrepreneur, but just saw something in the world, as many entrepreneurs do, that just didn't sit right. And I wanted to find a solution for that. So that was how I started. I think once I got the, not just entrepreneurial, but kind of the tech bug, I knew I was never going back to kind of traditional, you know, law, finance, all that kind of stuff. Like it was just in my blood and I was so excited just about, you know, how you can make an impact in the future. And so I started another company and unfortunately that one was not as successful. But I actually think, you know, looking back, I probably learned a lot more from that second one. I learned a lot from the first one because I'd made a lot of mistakes, but, you know, my biggest attribute I think was timing. And as many entrepreneurs know, a lot of things are out of your control and, you know, market tailwinds, oftentimes, you know, you have nothing to do with them. But we got pretty lucky the first time. I'd say those tailwinds turned into headwinds for our second company, which was actually a really good idea. And I've seen many companies go on to great success kind of, you know, around a similar space. was a text message marketing company. But at the time in 2010, you know, many of your younger listeners won't even be able to relate, but I think you will. It was a little bit like offensive to get marketing on your phone. Your phone was this like very personal thing where you called your mother. And it really wasn't, you know, the supercomputer that we all have that we're glued to where we can do anything. And many people like honestly run their whole businesses on their phone, right? It really just wasn't that. And unfortunately, it was just a timing issue. Like we had a lot of good things. We had a lot of great team members. We had, you know, good backers. We had a lot of good, you know, got a product roadmap. But we just couldn't get people to kind of get over that psychology of it being intrusive. Well, now, I

[None]
mean,

[SPEAKER_01]
like what people get on their phones, like can't even, you know, can't even talk about. So, you know, that's just an example of being at the wrong side of a trend or, you know, just, you know, too early.

[None]
Well, let's go back.

[SPEAKER_00]
Jane, let's go back to the first company. What was that?

[None]
That was. Yeah.

[SPEAKER_01]
So the story is I had a boyfriend in Germany. I was making lots of international phone calls. And my mobile phone bill was about $1,000 a month. So very different than, you know, now calling again. Different time, 2007. And I looked around. I was working at J.P. Morgan at the time. And there were all these bankers that were actually not from the U.S. And they were calling friends and family. And they were using these, like, calling cards. I mean, these are people working at J.P. Morgan. And, like, they were also, like, going down to the little bodegas and getting their little calling cards. So I just thought, wow, like, there's a few different use cases here. And yet the technology is just so antiquated. And so, you know, could we create something to automate essentially what a calling card would do through an application on your phone? The iPhone had just launched. And all of a sudden, you know, we could do a lot more on our mobile devices. So, again, started out solving a personal problem I had calling the boyfriend and turned into, you know, a really kind of impactful company. Because now people, instead of, you know, paying, you know, hundreds of dollars a month to call their loved ones back in countries that they came from, they could literally do that for a few dollars. And so that was just this, like, kind of incredible moment where you could, like, really help people, you know, change their daily experience.

[SPEAKER_00]
That's great. Thank you for clarifying. That's really interesting. All right. So bring us back to where you saw the second one, second company, not so great. Then what did

[None]
you do?

[SPEAKER_01]
to shut it down. I was working on my third company and, you know, somehow ended up on the other side. So, you know, I thought I was going to take some time off. I was going to go on some big travels. But I ended up, you know, at a venture fund called Techstars. And when I met the founders of Techstars, they had thought, they said, you know, do you ever thought about kind of being on the other side and investing? Which I had. But I was really kind of thinking about my next company. And they said, yeah, come spend a year or with us. And I think you'll learn the other side. And I think what I really loved about that platform is it wasn't just about cash. It was really about community and resources. And that was the thing that was most lacking in my entrepreneurial, you know, journey. Because, again, I came from New York City, not Silicon Valley. At the time, there was just, like, no community here, which is, like, hard for people to believe because it's, you know, second largest tech ecosystem. But there just wasn't. There weren't co -working spaces. There wasn't venture capitalists. There weren't meetups. mean, there was just, like, nothing going on. And everyone said, if you're going to build a software company, you need to go out west. But I kind of looked around and I said, like, that doesn't exactly make sense to me. Because if you look at all of the pieces that we had in New York, it seemed like a great place to build a company. There wasn't that community. But, I mean, we had capital. We didn't have venture capital. But we had, you know, lots of rich people, Wall Street, you know, real estate people. So it's like, you know, there was a lot of money sloshing around. We have every multinational here that you could sell to or partner with. Incredible engineering schools where great talent was coming out. I mean, you know, New York had so much to offer. And yet people were saying you had to go to California. And I thought, that's, like, really weird. So I was definitely one of the earlier people building companies here. And, you know, it was really fun back then. It was a small community. And it was just, you know, kind of the beginning.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. And so I remember that. Oh, God. Through the years, just going into the city. was so exciting. I remember meeting Marissa Meyer at some meetup.

[None]
It

[SPEAKER_00]
was just one distant memory. But early days. So then you went from Techstars to what?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So the other kind of through line in my journey is that I tend to kind of bootstrap things. So while I, you know, bootstrapped my first company, was working at J.P. Morgan and started that company nights and weekends, I did the same thing with my fund. So I was working at Techstars, kind of came up with the thesis for everywhere based on my entrepreneurial journeys, coupled with, you know, many years working with entrepreneurs, you know, through the accelerator model. And I thought,

[None]
hmm,

[SPEAKER_01]
maybe I could come up with some type of hybrid where, you know, we had a lot of the kind of community and ethos of maybe an angel group. But we had the structure and governance of a venture capital firm. And so we came up with, you know, the concept of our fund, which is unique in that we are backed by all founders and operators. So the people that give us money, our limited partners, are other builders. And we've got 500 of them. And so that large community is what not only fuels our deal flow, but really helps us support our large portfolio. So we, you know, tried to come up with a hybrid. We looked at venture capital and we said, like, what do we think is working and not working? And can we iterate on a model that seemed a little static?

[SPEAKER_00]
That's great. And so this was started up during the pandemic then, right?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, 2000. Well, we actually started in 2018. We did a proof of concept fund. And then we launched our second fund in 2020. So kind of, you know, right during the pandemic, which was delightful. And yeah, we've been going ever since. You know, I was, again, bootstrapped it. So like we were part time. My co -founder and I both had other jobs. And so we were working on our fund part time. And then in 2022, I decided to leave Techstars. My co -founder joined me and we decided to kind of launch a proper fund. And so our last fund was in 2022.

[None]
Got it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And everywhere. How did you come up with that name?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, it's definitely gone through some iterations. But, you know, our first fund was really focused on New York. That was the ecosystem we were living in and, you know, where I'd built companies before. And the thesis was like, if we could find 50, you know, great founders, if they could become our limited partners, people that give us money and our source of deal flow, like we could really see a lot. And so the second iteration of the fund was like, OK, if this works in New York, maybe it'll work in London and maybe it'll work in L.A. and maybe it'll work in Sydney, Australia. So we started to partner with entrepreneurs around the world to kind of spin up these nodes of founders, both that wanted to be investors, because many of them were angel investors and who wanted to kind of join our community as portfolio. So it just, you know, like I always tell people, I mean, we've been doing this almost seven years. It's just like you can't run a global fund overnight. You have to just spend years and years developing, you know, these networks and these nodes and cultivating them and nurturing them. And so, you know, at some point we looked around and we said, wow, we've got, you know, probably 30 of these communities around the world. They're somewhat self -organizing, but we get really great deal flow, really great intel. They help us with diligence, with sourcing, with supporting, you know, why does it actually matter where these companies are being built? And so we kind of looked at, you know, our geographic mandate and we said, honestly, like, we don't really care where founders are based. You know, we believe innovation's everywhere. Capital traditionally has been constrained to a few places, but like now that's really opening up. And where is a company based if one founder is in Austin, Texas, one is in London and one is in Singapore? Like, I don't know. So like why have geographic constraints? So we felt like the name everywhere really encapsulated our ethos and kind of the way that we see the world.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I love that. And talk to us a bit more about your thesis and what types of checks you cut. What are you looking for?

[None]
Yeah,

[SPEAKER_01]
so we invest at the pre -seed, which we define as small rounds, typically about 500K to 2 million. So not the Silicon Valley, like I'm raising a $10 million pre -seed. So these are small, modest rounds, oftentimes, you know, first time founders, but, you know, not always. But really that kind of foundational capital that helps, you know, really get the business off the ground. Our deal flow comes from this community of 500 founders and operators. So as you can imagine, we see lots of different types of companies and verticals and business models. So that's really exciting. As we, you know, started investing over the years, we started to like look at patterns and where some of our top performers were coming and like couple that with like where we see the world. And so I would say, you know, we're focused on software, although we're somewhat agnostic in terms of the areas that we invest in. What we like to say is that we invest in what we call the resilience economy. And so what that means is what's the technologies, the software, the infrastructure that's making certain verticals, you know, more viable and more resilient. For instance, like we're not investing in healthcare delivery, so to speak, but we invest a ton in healthcare infrastructure rather. Maybe it's on the EHR side, electronic medical records, or maybe it's, you know, underlying AI models that help, you know, clinicians, you know, assess information, you know, more effectively. So what's the technologies that make those verticals really hum? And so I'd say we do a lot in kind of fintech, climate, logistics, future of work, and of course, healthcare. But again, really somewhat agnostic as long as it's that kind of foundational infrastructure layer.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And what, since you're all around the world, well, first of all, you have 500 LPs. Do they think they have sort of preferences if they send you deal flow? Or do you sort of lay down the law and say, it's going through the system?

[SPEAKER_01]
I mean, I think the system, they are the system. So what's really cool is like, if I get a healthcare deal that comes to me from you or from anyone in the community, I can like on our Slack channel very quickly send it out to 50 of our LPs that are all in and around the healthcare space and get a directional read of like, hey, you know, what do you think of this? And within 30 minutes, I have, you know, like so many people getting back and saying, oh, Jenny, there are a million of these, or this is really interesting. Here are a few questions you should ask. And so like, you know, we use them as a source of, you know, information and diligence and see that as a real asset. So, yeah. But I think, you know, people are very understanding just in terms of, you know, we can't invest in all the companies that come through the pipe. But I would say everything that gets to us has already been like layer one filtered because these folks are all builders. They're building companies and they've got kind of a good view on things like product and business model, as opposed to stuff that comes randomly through our website, which we do get a lot of that as well.

[SPEAKER_00]
Right. And what about leveraging AI to screen? Are you using those tools or are there good tools yet to help with that sort of tedious, you know, when you get thousands of ventures every year?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, we've spent the last, you know, seven years building kind of a stack of collaborative tools that allow us as our fund to be more efficient. So, for instance, like way before the pandemic, we made a decision that like the Monday morning partner meeting, right, where everyone gathers was like somewhat antiquated. My co -founder lives in LA. You know, we have some teammates in Europe, in New York. And so could we do a lot of our work async? And so we really relied on Slack and some of, you know, the other software tools like Airtable to allow us to go through our process in a really effective way, not necessarily gathering. So my point is that we've spent many years and, you know, lots of time kind of thinking through lots of automations that allows us to invest in, you know, high, you know, a lot of companies in a short amount of time. So we've invested in 300 companies and we're two general partners. And everyone says like, well, how do you do that? And that's through a lot of the automations that we've built. So, you know, has AI been transformational for our company? Not necessarily. mean, we've been using kind of basic, you know, automations to, you know, synchronize our business for the last, you know, six, seven years. But it is exciting, obviously, with some of the tools now to make things like deal memos and, you know, some of our kind of internal data more efficient. So I'd say like, it's exciting to have those tools. It hasn't been transformational for us yet because we've already, you know, we've always kind of used a lot of that.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And what about, since you are all around the world, what trends or where are the hotspots? Is there any sort of indicators you're seeing that are sort of really interesting?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. I mean, we do a fair amount in Africa. I'd say mostly Nigeria and South Africa. We see obviously a lot of fintech and infrastructure coming out of those communities. What's exciting about them is sometimes where you don't have a lot of legacy infrastructure like you do here, you can institute new technologies, you know, much, much quicker with less, you know, less red tape in some ways. So there's obviously challenges of doing businesses in places like that. We do a lot in Latam as well, specifically Brazil and Mexico. But the speed at which, you know, you can, you know, implement something at a big company, we just don't really see here because we have so much kind of, you know, legacy software debt in all of our companies and our government that you can't just like rip things in and out, right? It takes like years to integrate them. So it is exciting in developing countries how fast, you know, some of the implementations can work.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And what do you see? I know you teach at universities and you're active in the, you know, some of the entrepreneurial programs. What are you seeing there? What's sort of piquing your interest and some of the things or trends you've seen over the years?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, I mean, it's fun. You know, while I was at Techstars, we worked on an application basis. And for my programs, I'd get, you know, a few thousand applications. So you get to see, you know, in mass, like what entrepreneurs are thinking about. It's very similar at the university. So I co -head the startup studio at Cornell Tech on Roosevelt Island. And there's about 400 students in the startup studio class. And so they're all coming up with ideas, building startups over, you know, the course of the semester or the year. And you definitely see kind of these waves as new technologies get rolled out. So it's been fun to see like the evolution from, you know, crypto to AI. And you just see like so many, you know, so many cool, you know, variations of what can be right. These students are very, very creative. I'd say in this last batch, we've seen a lot of like, I'd call it workflow automations. You know, people are really bored with, you know, boring tasks or they're really sick of boring tasks, I should say. And we're seeing a lot of students trying to make, you know, simple things like campus life or, you know, all the all these, you know, their calendars or whatnot more efficient. And so that's been that's been really fun because I always think about like, oh, you know, when I was a student and like, you know, when I had to sign up for classes or I had to do all these things. So we're seeing a lot of like workflow automation, I'd say, which is fun. We always see a lot of health care. And this year we've seen a lot in the kind of wellness and mental health space, which can kind of give you a sense of what students are are dealing with. Right. It's very stressful being, you know, being students at a lot of these campuses. Not just the academic stress, but, you know, just everything that's going on in the world. And students really want to, you know, be creating solutions for their peer group. And I think that's been really kind of interesting to see again, you know, going back to that empath founder building for themselves in their community. We see a lot of that on campus.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, that's really interesting. I'd be curious to see what's next, you know, what are they what's and you'll have a sort of a first peek at that. But what about the environment? Right. There obviously is this lot of anxiety and stress in the world today. How is that affecting sort of the funding environment? What do you I know it's impossible to forecast, but how do you see things?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So, I mean, obviously the tech bubble 2020 and 2022 are kind of some crazy days. I don't think they were very healthy. We struggled as a fund. And then we saw a drop off on a crash that also didn't seem healthy. Right. And so I think that we were hoping 2025 would get us back into some equilibrium. Right. So 2023, 2024 were very challenging fundraising environments, except for maybe a select group of, you know, infrastructure AI companies who were sucking up most of the cash. It was very, very challenging. So I think that, you know, what people were hopeful for with the new administration was things like liquidity coming to the market through more M &A, more IPOs. I think people were excited about that. You know, some of the crypto regulations getting sorted out also could bring, you know, some good liquidity and some new innovation. So I think there was like a lot of hope. You know, it is early to say, but, you know, here we are mid -March and it seems like, you know, the markets are a little shaken up by, you know, what's happening. And we're not really seeing that reflected this kind of calm return to normal in venture yet. So I don't know. I mean, we haven't seen a ton of IPOs. We haven't really seen much on the M &A. Still early days, but I think that was kind of the hope. So we'll see. To be determined, I'd say right now it feels kind of similar to 2024 and 2023, which is a bit of a have and have not, right? So some rounds gets on quite quickly, depending on the vertical, the team, the momentum that they build in the business. And some deals, which I think are great, just take forever to get done. They stagnate. And it's kind of hard to understand, like, which camp you're in. It's not, you know, these clear, like, check a box and you're in one camp. So I'd say it's still pretty binary and still pretty turbulent.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. Yeah. Time will tell, right? Right. What about the new book you have? I heard a rumor that you have a new book. Tell us about that.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So I wrote a book called Venture Everywhere. And the book talks about many of the journeys that I've just shared with you in the context of a larger framework of entrepreneurship. So the book is about global entrepreneurship, which is obviously the theme of my fund and what we can all learn from founders building companies far from the glow of Silicon Valley. And when I interviewed these entrepreneurs, I noticed some common themes and perspectives about the way they view the world, which I kind of distill into what I call this everywhere mindset. And it's, you know, kind of this, you know, these archetypes of, you know, how you build companies and how you, you know, prepare your mind for entrepreneurship, which is so intense. So the book is 12 chapters, 12 countries, 12 entrepreneurial journeys and people you might not have heard of, but they have gone on to, you know, have public companies to have huge exits. I mean, these are like really incredible entrepreneurs, but we hear about the same folks, right? Like we, we know a lot about Zuckerberg. We know a lot about Bill Gates. We know a lot about Elon Musk. And so it's really kind of a celebration of people who've come from very different backgrounds and how they've kind of persevered and the resilience that they've had to build the businesses that they've been able to build. And so what's that psychology and what are those kinds of traits that we can all learn from?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, that sounds exciting. And it really broadens people's perspective, right? We always hear the, you know, the Zuckerbergs and the Bezos

[None]
and we

[SPEAKER_00]
sometimes don't realize there's so many amazing entrepreneurs around the world, right?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah.

[None]
And also,

[SPEAKER_01]
I mean, you know, it's interesting. So I'd say the book is a pretty counter to, you know, the kind of current narrative in the U.S. right now. We seem to be going into more of like an isolationist mentality of like looking in. The book thesis is really that, you know, we're living in global times. And then if you don't kind of, you know, get prepared to be working with people around the world to kind of understand and have empathy for where they come from. And to have a global mindset, like, you know, you're going to be left behind. And I believe that that is 100 % true, you know, despite what's happening right now. Well, 20 years ago, you and I could work in an office and we might only interact with people from the U.S. There's no way that that's your experience now. Your customers, your teammates, just everyone is so global with distributed, you know, working and living. We have to kind of think about building companies and building, you know, our own resilience to be able to handle, you know, that kind of the global influences.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, for sure. And I'll put the link to the book in the show notes. So for folks who want to read it and learn more. But let's talk about that a bit more. So as we both know, global hubs, ecosystems have developed around the world, right? Especially from 20, 30 years ago, right? Now everyone has learned and sort of borrowed sort of the approaches that we've developed, at least in the States and other Western, you know, Western countries. So if you were to give advice to an entrepreneur in the U.S., where would you say, and they could live anywhere, let's just say anywhere in the U.S., would you recommend certain places or would you say, it doesn't matter, be close to your family?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, I think that you need to develop networks. And to do that, you need to spend time in different places with different people. And those networks, like once you kind of develop it, then I think you have the ability to, you know, run your company wherever you want to run it. So I think it's hard right now if you just like were starting a company and you were living in a very rural place and you had no community and no network. I do think that that is challenging. It's not impossible, but it is challenging. But really, like what's interesting about the book is that many of the founders, you know, come from very, you know, rural places. So one of the founders, he grew up in a small town in Pakistan. No one in his family had gone to and had any type of schooling. And his family like owned, you know, a small little neighborhood store. But they had big ambitions for the next generation and really like focused on, you know, getting them educated. He came to the U.S. Anyway, fast forward. He's built like the, you know, pretty much the most successful, I think, company in the Middle East that was sold to Uber for three billion dollars. Right. And so, you know, why this guy? Well, he built his networks. Right. He came to Silicon Valley. He lived in London. He went to Dubai. And he, you know, kind of built those relationships, that trust, that network that he could, you know, really, you know, have this kind of crazy, amazing story. And I think we all need to do that. So if I was an entrepreneur now, I think living in or near a tech hub, you know, at early days and developing those networks and making sure that you've, you know, got that community and those resources, but then I think you can live wherever you want. [None]

You know, the second order is a little more interesting. It's like, well, will you actually need VCs? In the same way that I think that conversation is happening, like, well, will you actually need lawyers and will you actually need any service providers? I don't really have the answer except to say that I'm open to the possibility that it all changes, whereas I feel like the lawyers are not open to that. When you tell, when I tell my lawyer friends that the whole empire that they've built may come crumbling down, they look at me like I'm crazy and they don't want to talk to me. Whereas, like, I feel more open to that as a possibility for venture capital, like, maybe I won't have a job in five years. And you know what, like, that's fine. I'll keep on building and going where the interesting opportunities are. So, you know, I think in the short term, not a ton is going to change except hopefully for the better that we have more time

freed up for

founders. In the long term, will there be kind of a marketplace using AI agents that doesn't really require me to be there, that efficient capital can be, you know, connected to great founders? Like, I'm open to that.

Hmm.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. Interesting. And, you know, I quickly want to do the top three. What's your favorite business book?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, this is kind of interesting. I just reread The Innovators by Walter Isaacson, and it's an old book, but it gave me a lot of inspiration for the future. So I sometimes think, like, going back and revisiting older books is pretty great.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. put that in the show notes. And, you know, if you could go back in time when you started Everywhere Ventures, what is the one thing you would have focused on or done differently?

[SPEAKER_01]
Oh, my gosh, that's a good question. I think we expanded pretty quickly. And with that, we covered a lot of ground. You feel the pull of different geographies. And all of a sudden, like, we wanted to be there. So maybe a little bit more planning on how we rolled out Everywhere Ventures everywhere.

[SPEAKER_00]
And

what's

We run our whole community on Slack.

have a thousand founders. We've exchanged more than one million Slack messages since we started it. And zero cat memes. It's all founder resources. So there's a lot of fancy tools out there. But that one is really critical for us.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. We'll put that in the show notes. And Jenny, what's the best way people can reach out to you and know more about your book?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, so you can connect with me on LinkedIn. And Venture Everywhere is out soon. So check it out on Amazon. And that's it. Follow me on Twitter.

I'm Chris Grew. I'm the CEO and founder of American Prison Data Systems. We are a New York City -based tech startup. We are also a public benefits corporation. Our mission is to provide tools to the folks who run America's very large, very expensive, and arguably dysfunctional correctional systems with tools that help them improve safety, the efficacy of their spend, and most importantly, that work towards delivering better outcomes for incarcerated people. Prior to this, I've been an entrepreneur of one kind or another in the U.S. K -12 educational publishing space, where I have started businesses and worked as an entrepreneur in residence at some large American publishing companies, including Scholastic, the Princeton Review, a handful of others, and I'm also proud to say I'm a Columbia alum.

[SPEAKER_06]
Okay. This is going to come up in a follow -up question for two of the entrepreneurs on the panel here in a second. But my sense is that because the investment community is sometimes so focused on what's hot today, as an entrepreneur, if you're actually really solving a problem for somebody, there's a pain point, but it's not the hot thing today, what recommendation would you provide in terms of how they communicate that to a potential investor VC to help them see the light?

[SPEAKER_03]
Yeah. I mean, I think an accelerator is a great way to go because we're not really looking for those hot trends. We're looking for entrepreneurs. So we always say, you know, we invest in these six things in this order, team, team, team, product, you know, market, and, you know, a few other things. So, you know, we're really looking for awesome teams of entrepreneurs, and I think that that affords the opportunity to, you know, differentiate yourself with something that's ahead of the curve. So I think, you know, if you go with early -stage investors like us, we're really willing to look beyond the traditional.

[None]
Great. Thank you.

[SPEAKER_06]
Ximena, OKCupid. It's always great to have somebody from a dating service on a panel. So many

[None]
questions people

[SPEAKER_06]
want me to ask you, right? But my sense is that when you come to a dating site and you're getting it launched, there can be a tendency to gravitate towards what society views as a typical dating profile or the typical type of person who's going to ask somebody out and who wants to be asked out by them. But in fact, especially in the United States and especially in major urban areas, there's a lot of diversity out there in terms of preferences, what people are looking for. And, you when it's online, there's a lot more flexibility and confidence that someone can have. What did you guys do at OKCupid to make sure you didn't gravitate towards, let's just facilitate something for the status quo dating or the stereotype dating? And how do we make this more expansive to get business in from lots of diverse groups and their preferences?

[SPEAKER_02]
So I'm going to start with dating tips because I'm sure you're going to find them interesting. In terms of we actually found on OKCupid that there's, of course, a lot of people that get a lot of likes. That's the people that, on average, everyone thinks that they're good looking. Those people will get X number of messages. But what is really interesting is the people that are found to be polarizing. So either a big set of people will think they're really bad looking and other people will think that they're really good looking. The reason is that the people that find them really good looking will find them so compelling. It's almost like they find that special match that no one else could see that they had all this potential. So when we talk about what are recommendations for our profiles is that it should not be the thing that you think everyone will like. You need to write about the things that make you different. Like from all the quirks of, like myself, I like to do hand crafting for jewelry or things that are just a bit odd. And then there might be someone that really, that resonates with them. So that's the part about if a profile is detailed, it has more chances of getting that special someone that just is intrigued by the thing that you're writing, even if it's a little bit weird. The second part is about not just going by the masses. So at OKCupid, I'll talk about it a little bit later, we took the stance to also launch 22 genders and 13 orientations. And that was a big decision from the business side because we knew that it was not going to be used by a lot of people and most of the dating is just going to be men, women, and then gay, straight, and bisexual. But then we decided that if it's something so important to people, like who's going to be the person that you might marry, you need to use the words that feel appropriate. So when someone in Kansas, a boy that is 18 years old, can write questioning sexuality, all of a sudden it has the people when they see it, it's something that it's OK. And then you can say, well, there's so many things about my sexuality that I'm still figuring out. Or in terms of genders, these are all the different genders I align with. So that was more from when you're thinking of a business, it's not for everyone, but it's also about the social responsibility that you have towards the people so that you're advancing towards where society is going and that sometimes it's not just about the bottom line or revenue, but what should be good.

They churn their cleaning operators a lot every year, but then there's also huge operator churn. We call everyone operators at Q. Huge operator churn every year, and we realized that those two things were connected. So you couldn't solve one problem without also trying to solve the other problem. So at Q, we decided to take on trying to create a better work experience for the operator, and that would actually create a better client experience, and the two are linked. So it's not that we go out to the clients and say, hey, our operators are not going to do X. What we've done is we invested in a, you know, it's called a good job strategy. We invested in a program where we invested in sort of recruiting, training, and then developing our operators within their various service lines, and then we looked at technology to help them do their jobs better and also how to communicate back and forth with, you know, oh, I'm going to be late because the subway's down. It's not that you're late. It's that you can communicate to the client that you're going to be late or you are unable to perform a task, so it's not like you're leaving the office space with a task unperformed. The client then knows through technology that, oh, this task was performed because the dishwasher was broken. So it's combining technology not only for the service of the client but also for the service of the operator to make the whole thing work better.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_06]

[SPEAKER_07]

And what we looked at is, hey, by investing more money up front to create a better product and a better experience for our employees, we're actually then able to spend that money on growing the business, not replacing the business lost.

[None]
Great. Related

to that, Christopher, just so everyone's clearly aware, your core market are hardcore prisoners, right? People have been put away because of something bad that they did in society. And you've decided to design a product and service that is going to help them rehabilitate themselves and be more productive citizens in society. Sounds like a big waste of time. These guys completely screwed up. They're sitting in prison. What do you think in trying to give them a tablet and technology to do something with?

[SPEAKER_00]
Oh, there's a lot there. The first thing is, you know, America incarcerates more people than any civilization has in its history, more than the gulag state. And it's a mixed bag of who ends up incarcerated. There are 2.2 million people behind bars today, another 5.5 million on parole or probation, which means 1 out of every 31 adults in the United States is behind bars. And for every Charles Manson that we lock up and never want to see again and I've sort of given up on, there are lots and lots and lots of folks who've just made bad decisions, ended up in bad circumstances, and hopefully have a bright future ahead of them. And the mission of our business is to, to the maximum extent possible, give people a second chance. The vast majority of people who are incarcerated in the United States will be released and they will be back living with us and we'll see them on the subway. And it's in everyone's best interest that they have the tools that they need to succeed. And so what we're trying to do is use technology to deliver individualized education, rehabilitation, job training, and re -entry skills so that folks who have made bad decisions and maybe have been left behind by the school system or other parts of society have an opportunity to start their lives again. And I'm struck by some of the congruences and possible opportunities to work together with Jimmy's business and with Chris's. So, one, we shouldn't give up on these folks. Two, they're extremely, it's an extremely diverse set. And what we need to do as a mission of our business is, paradoxically, we have taken a large bunch of people who have a very diverse set of education, rehabilitation, job training, and re -entry needs, and we've isolated them in the last part of American society where technology cannot reach them. And we've sort of unintentionally put a digital mode around them, which is separating them from the kinds of programs that could really make a difference in their lives. So the mission of our business has been to build a bridge across that mode to allow all of the wonderful things that technology can do, all of those educational programs, to drive across that bridge, but also at the same time safeguard public safety by making sure that, you we don't have inmates on Twitter or on Facebook or even OKCupid, I'm sorry to say, until they're out and released and then that might be a good thing for them to be doing with their time.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_06]
let's talk dollars and cents, right, because you're a for -profit venture. How much does it cost to incarcerate somebody in the United States?

[SPEAKER_00]
Let's start top down. The direct cost of incarceration in the United States are at least $85 billion annually. We've already talked about the numbers of people we incarcerate. So locking up that many people and spending $85 billion a year averages $30,000, $35,000 a year to incarcerate someone, depending on where you are. Here in New York City, it's at least $110,000 a year. In

[None]
Mississippi, it's a little expensive than going

[SPEAKER_06]
to Columbia.

[None]
It's much more expensive than going

[SPEAKER_00]
to Columbia. And all of that might be OK if the system, quote -unquote, worked. And what do we mean by working in corrections? Making the public safer and hopefully changing lives where that's possible. We have a 43 % recidivism rate in this country, which means of the 800,000 people who will be released from prison in the United States, 43 % of them will be back in prison within three years. So it's not working. And though we have dramatically increased the number of people that we've incarcerated, we have not seen concomitant improvements in public safety or decreases in violence. So what we're doing isn't working, and it's expensive. And so our goal is to be disruptive and to create new tools. The folks who run our correctional institutions are, in general, very well motivated to give the public what they want. They just haven't had the tools to do that. And that's where I see a for -profit, for -purpose business sort of getting in.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_06]
it costs $100,000 in New York City to keep somebody in prison. What are you charging the system to provide education and professional training services to this person so that when they get out of prison, they're not returning because you've given them the skills?

[SPEAKER_00]
We're in 20 locations across the country. I'm very proud to say that one of those locations is Rikers Island. I'll get very specific about that. We work with all of the juveniles who are in something called East River Academy, which is a high school that's run on Rikers Island. And though the most concrete version of our business is people say, oh, you sell tablets. Well, we are, in fact, we are a software -as -a -service business. And what matters is not the device itself, but the content that's delivered. And it's very important because this is sort of brass tack stuff. We have to sit down on day one and say, if you invest $1,000 in a software -as -a -service license seat for this inmate, let me show you how that will save you, Mr. Warden, $3,000 in the first year. And that's enough to get over the first threshold. Over time, we hope to have the longitudinal data that suggests that we get at the real cost center and the real benefit, that is we're reducing recidivism. And a 5%, 10 % decrease in recidivism in this country would save state and local and federal institutions and taxpayers billions of dollars. Okay, great. Thank you.

[SPEAKER_06]
Jimmy, I'd like to

[None]
bring

that. Okay.

[None]
I

[SPEAKER_02]
actually had a point exactly around that. That was, I've lately been seeing a lot of trends on companies that could do things more efficiently. But I think I'm

[SPEAKER_02]
even more interested in, I've been talking, I talked last week with the CEO of a company called Joyable, and they do mental health programs. Well, in the same way, they can do programs now that allow you to talk about the problems that you could have and over time accomplish a lot of the, it's almost like going to therapy without actually having to even go outside of your door and they're trying to reach people that don't even want to talk about the problems that they have. Yeah, so let me start with the size of the program. There are 45 million Americans on food stamps today, so every table in this room has about seven chairs. That's about one chair at every table is somebody who's on food stamps. Combined, the food stamp program is about $70 billion each year. This is money that ends up being spent at grocery stores. about 12 % of the American retail grocery industry is actually food stamps. It's a huge industry because there are a ton of people who kind of experience it, and their day -to -day experience with the program turns out is not very good. Now, I think if you've gone to the DMV or applied for a visa, you probably have a sense that, you know, interacting with a government website or filling out a paper form can be really frustrating. I can tell you the same is true for a single mother who's trying to apply for food stamps or somebody who has benefits and is trying to understand how to best use their food stamps. So our core product is actually just a smartphone app. It's an app called Fresh EBT that works a little bit like mint.com for people on food stamps. So it helps people understand their current balance to see their transaction histories and to create these budgets that help them stretch their benefits to where they want to be. Our business comes from helping our users to discover other products and services that make them more physically and financially healthy. And so there's kind of two categories of that. The first one are kind of grocery stores. So last month, our users spent about $40 million combined in food stamps at grocery stores. How do we use that combined purchasing power to get them savings on the food that they're already going to purchase? Our second business model is financial service referrals. So we have a population that's traditionally preyed on pretty significantly by the financial services industry. But we think there's a large and growing segment of companies out there building pro -social financial services that can replace some of these old, stodgy financial services that would just aim to rip people off. So these are things like online replacements for payday loans or for check cashing or for title loans. How do we introduce our users to those things in a way that makes them more financially healthy?

So I see an interesting thread taking place here. think oftentimes when you go to a lot of panel discussions about entrepreneurship to the earlier point about most people are trying to solve problems that are issues for themselves or their friends. And they may be masked in, like, I'm changing the world. In fact, they're just trying to make their life a little bit better. I see an interesting thread here where there are millions of Americans who are in the prison system that have no experience with technology. If you have no experience with technology, it's going to be hard for you to be a productive person in society. A lot of the folks that are coming out of the prison system at first may need to be on food stamps. The challenge is they may not have the comfort level in terms of how to apply for something, how to use technology. And now there's a business model that can help service that. In all seriousness, you get out of prison, you need to build a social network and you need to find a partner. And there's online networks to do that. But if you don't know how to use technology, you're out of it now. And then there's job opportunities. So it's interesting to see how just putting that seed in there

[None]
allows the ecosystem

[SPEAKER_06]
to be

[None]
built.

[SPEAKER_00]

I've been collecting in my mind the numbers of jobs that you simply can't do if you don't understand technology. And let's be clear, 40 blocks from here is an institution called The Castle, which is run by the Fortune Society, where folks who've spent more than 10 or 15 years in New York State prisons come and spend a year before fully reintegrating into society. Those folks have never owned a smartphone, never had a tablet. The world has completely changed. And I have a listing in my mind of all of the very basic sort of entry -level jobs you simply cannot do in the society. Can't work for FedEx, can't work at a grocery store stocking a shelf if you don't know what one of these guns are, how to operate an Android tablet. So there are a lot of affinities. I see one other sort of connecting point, which is there are things that government wants to do, and actually only government can give $70 billion in food to single moms and others. But they often cannot go the last mile or the last yard with regards to technology to getting it right. All of their websites are kludgy. They don't have a budget line to build an app or to make that last connection. so the question is, can you help government achieve its goals and still start a great business? And I think you can. And increasingly, these double bottom line businesses that identify compelling pain points and sort of an unmet need and a gap and disruptively making money while doing well, doing good, I see lots of successful businesses in that space. And I commend you, Jimmy. I think what you're doing is incredibly important. And everyone who leaves prison needs to know about his site.

[None]
And I

[SPEAKER_03]
can tell you also, from an aggregate of our hundreds of thousands of applications that we get, every year increasingly more double bottom line. So if you look at my last FinTech class, we had 10 companies. We had two that had an angle that were socially responsible, sustainable. Now I have an Internet of Things program. And one of the new areas is around smart cities, right? Which was a term that really we had a few years ago, right? And so these new verticals, I think, are popping up that do have, you know, a social element. And we're seeing that reflected in the entrepreneurs that we're funding.

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah, and even for the government, I think that even though it has taken them a bit of time, they recently recruited Megan Smith, who is the CTO of the United States.

[None]
And in one panel

[SPEAKER_02]
like this one, I actually met the chief data officer of the Department of Commerce. And it turns out that I was actually talking about the different genders that OkCupid had had. Hello and welcome to today's episode of Authentic Achievements, where it's my absolute privilege to be joined by the fabulous Jenny Fielding. Jenny, hello. Hi, thanks for having me. So Jenny is one of the most active global pre -seed investors, having invested in over 300 companies as the first money in. As the co -founder and managing partner of Everywhere Ventures, Jenny has built a thriving community of 500 plus founders and operators who help source, diligence and invest in the next generation of startups across three core verticals, money, health and work. Prior to launching her own fund, Jenny spent seven and a half years as the managing director of Techstars, where she invested in a portfolio of companies with a current market cap of over 10 billion. Jenny is a two times founder, a lawyer by training and an adjunct professor at Columbia University and Cornell Tech and author, which I'd love to for you to tell us more about. But I've traveled around the world, lived around the world and, you know, had some

[None]
interesting journeys,

[SPEAKER_01]
which I'll talk about later in the book. But I started much more, let's call it traditional for someone who grows up in New York. I went to law school, I worked in finance, and I was kind of on on a track. And then in 2007, so about 15 years ago, I had a problem, like a personal thing that I wanted to solve in the world. And then all of a sudden, that plan changes. Life throws you a plot twist and something else comes along. But could you tell me a little bit about that first startup? [None]
third startup,

it was really about making sure you have the right building blocks in place. And I think that's really important.

I love it. the

documents.text:
[SPEAKER_02]
Hello and welcome back to Equity, TechCrunch's flagship podcast about the business of startups. I'm Haya, and today is our Wednesday episode. We're bringing deep dive conversations back to the podcast on Wednesdays, and today we're taking a look at what some are calling the Series A cliff. To give us some context, we'll be talking to Jenny Fielding, co -founder and managing partner at Everywhere Ventures. Jenny, welcome back to the show.

[None]
Thanks so much

[SPEAKER_01]
for having me. Excited to be here.

[SPEAKER_02]
Jenny's been on Equity before, talking about how startups have to double down on quality, and how smaller firms can compete with their more established peers, and much more. That's not what we're talking about today, however. It's rough out there for startups, and Jenny, you put out a tweet which sparked a whole bunch of debate. What exactly is the Series A cliff?

[None]
Yeah,

[SPEAKER_01]
I'm actually calling it the chasm. That's my new report. So essentially, it's much harder to raise a Series A right now. The bar has just moved, right? And so I think what founders are feeling is that while back in 2020, 2021, you could get to something like a million dollars in ARR and be able to raise a proper Series A from a great Series A fund. There was a lot of variables on that, what area you're building in, your team background, all those things. But let's just call that general. And fast forward to today, where the goalposts have really moved. And so the tweet was really what I'm kind of seeing, which is the million has now gone up to sometimes three million. And let's not just talk about absolute numbers. There's also a growth rate that these investors are looking at. So it's really a tough moment for founders because they may have raised with different expectations, and now all of a sudden, the game has changed.

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah. Awesome. In your tweet, you specifically mentioned 30 % month -on -month growth, which is super aggressive, obviously. I feel like Y Combinator is pushing for 15 % week -on -week growth, which is obviously even wilder. But the compound growth in that is, I mean, that is crazy amounts of growth. Is that really the bottom end of where you're able to raise?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, I think, and many people pointed out in the tweet that if you compound that out a few years, we're talking about billions, right? And so I think what these VCs want to see is in a snapshot, in a cohort, that there is impressive growth.

[SPEAKER_02]
Right.

[SPEAKER_01]
Let me walk through a scenario because I think that that would be helpful. So oftentimes we'll see founders are getting started and maybe they bootstrap, maybe they do an accelerator, maybe they raise an angel round, they raise a small amount, a few hundred K, right? That gives them, call it 12 months to build an MVP. Then you have, we'll call it the institutional pre -seed. That's where I come in. And so let's say they raise, you know, another 1.5 and that gives them another 18 months and that gets them to a small amount of revenue. Now that small amount of revenue, few hundred thousand ARR, it's not enough to raise a series A. So they go out and they raise a seed. This all sounds reasonable. That gives them, you know, another 18 months and maybe they can get to a hundred K MRR. Now, if you take all the time and add it up of what I've just mentioned, right? So you've got kind of angel accelerator around the pre -seed and the seed, we're already at four years in and now they're getting to some revenue, like let's call it a little over a million. Well, you can't raise a series A on a million, as I mentioned. So now we need to raise another round and we'll call that a seed plus. And so maybe they raise a few million and that gives them another 18 months. So now we're five and a half years in to starting the company and maybe they're at two million ARR. And let's say that that is enough. Maybe they're at closer to three. Great. They're still five and a half years in. So even though the metric would say like, okay, you're doing two and a half million, like that should be enough for a series A. Some of the VCs are coming back and saying, well, this is a slow growth business. This isn't going to move the needle for me. We're not going to see the type of momentum that we need to see. So all of a sudden, it's not just about absolutes of revenue, but it's about time to get there.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_01]
so in that scenario, which we see in our portfolio all the time, we're talking about over five years from inception through to getting a series A done. So I call that the chasm.

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah, no, totally. I get that. Do you see this across every industry or are there certain verticals that are more challenging than others?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, I mean, the elephant in the room is maybe that's not all AI companies, although it kind of depends where in the stack you're playing in AI. But yeah, a lot of the trends are lagging indicators, right? So when we see things in the public markets tank, maybe like FinTech, all of a sudden, it's hard to get a FinTech deal done. But the truth is, like, we're not looking at what an exit opportunity would be today. We're looking at 10 years.

[None]
So like,

[SPEAKER_01]
I'm bullish on FinTech, why I love to talk to Marianne, because I'm looking at exit opportunities that are going to happen a long time. And do I think that that's where the world is going? The answer for me is yes. So it definitely is industry specific to a certain extent. But I haven't looked at the data, maybe you have, I feel like this series A chasm is really happening across industries, even industries that we don't invest in. I've heard that biotech is really challenging right now.

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah, mean, I feel like the numbers back that up, right? I looked at numbers from PitchBook and Crunchbase and DoxSend. And seed companies so far this year have raised about $7 billion, which is down a billion year on year. And in general, you know, especially at the later stages, it's down significantly. So it's really challenging, you know, the numbers from Crunchbase kind of seem to think that this is like an extended adolescence almost, where you have to get to a much more sensible place. And at the same time, this seems to kind of reflect a desire for VCs to get to a place of lower risk, right? And at that point, I'm like, wait, this doesn't seem like venture anymore, right? If all the risk is designed out of the company. Like I, I work with a lot of founders who get very exasperated. And the general battle cry is like, okay, well, VCs are cowards at the moment for not backing actual risky companies. Does that ring true for you at all?

[SPEAKER_01]
